paragraphs: Vision-language models can produce text that does not match the image they are describing. Some decoding methods try to reduce these hallucinations by comparing token scores under different visual conditions. Their effectiveness depends on making unsupported tokens distinguishable from appropriate ones. The paper argues that introducing broad visual uncertainty gives insufficient control over this distinction and can even encourage unwanted hallucinations.

The authors introduce Hallucination-Induced Optimization, or HIO, following a theoretical analysis of contrastive decoding. HIO uses a fine-tuned preference model called the Contrary Bradley-Terry Model to increase the separation between hallucinatory and targeted tokens. The central idea is to deliberately strengthen the contrast that decoding relies on, making its corrective signal more useful.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks report reduced hallucinations and better performance than the state-of-the-art methods evaluated. These findings support the value of optimizing how hallucinations are exposed during contrastive decoding: a more controlled comparison can help the model select text that better corresponds to its visual input.
neurips-2024-alleviating-hallucinations-.tldr: HIO reduces visual hallucinations by learning to sharpen the token-score contrast used in contrastive decoding.

paragraphs: LeapAD addresses autonomous driving through two complementary decision processes inspired by human cognition. It first selects objects that matter for driving decisions, reducing the complexity of interpreting the scene. This attention mechanism supports a broader effort to improve reasoning and adaptability in situations that existing driving methods find difficult.

An Analytic Process performs detailed reasoning and collects driving experience expressed in language. A Heuristic Process handles faster decisions and learns from that experience through supervised fine-tuning. Reflection and an expanding memory bank let the system use previous mistakes to improve subsequent behavior in a closed-loop environment, where its actions affect what happens next.

In closed-loop CARLA testing, LeapAD outperformed the camera-only methods evaluated while requiring one to two orders of magnitude less labeled data. Experiments also showed that a 1.8-billion-parameter Heuristic Process could inherit knowledge from a GPT-4-powered Analytic Process and improve as memory grew. The results demonstrate this transfer within the reported driving experiments, connecting detailed reasoning with a smaller decision-making model.
neurips-2024-continuously-learning-adapt.tldr: LeapAD transfers reflective driving experience from a reasoning process to a smaller, faster process that improves through accumulated memory.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation lets a deployed model adjust to the data it encounters. CoLA extends this idea across multiple devices, allowing their adaptation experience to accumulate in shared domain knowledge vectors. These vectors give devices access to information learned elsewhere during continued use, and the framework can be combined with existing adaptation methods.

CoLA assigns different adaptation strategies according to computational resources and latency needs. Principal agents learn new domain-specific parameters while also learning how to reweight existing shared knowledge. Follower agents use domain similarity to combine stored knowledge without performing optimization. This division gives devices a way to benefit from adaptation even when they cannot afford the same learning workload.

Experiments report improvements in efficiency and performance across collaborative, lifelong, and single-domain settings. On ImageNet-C, follower agents achieved an accuracy improvement of over 30% while maintaining nearly standard inference efficiency. The result illustrates the practical value of sharing adaptation knowledge: its benefits can reach devices that perform only lightweight aggregation.
neurips-2024-cross-device-collaborative-.tldr: CoLA shares adaptation knowledge across devices so lightweight agents can benefit without running their own optimization.

paragraphs: Multi-task offline reinforcement learning seeks one policy that can handle several tasks using previously collected experience. A central difficulty is deciding what to share across tasks: useful common structure must coexist with task-specific requirements, while conflicting learning signals can complicate training. DPDT addresses this problem through prompts that separate shared and specialized information.

The model starts from pretrained language-model parameters and uses two stages. During training, it learns both cross-task prompts and task-specific prompts. This decomposition provides a shared starting point without requiring every task to use an identical prompt. At test time, the cross-task prompt initializes further optimization for an unseen task, providing a parameter-efficient route to adaptation.

Evaluations on a collection of meta-reinforcement-learning benchmarks report superior performance for the approach. The findings support the usefulness of learning an adaptable shared prompt alongside specialized prompts. Its unseen-task performance involves test-time adaptation: the shared knowledge supplies an initialization that is refined for the new task.
neurips-2024-decomposed-prompt-decision-.tldr: DPDT separates shared and task-specific prompts, then adapts the shared prompt to improve performance on unseen reinforcement-learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a simplified model for analyzing trained neural networks and their sometimes surprising behavior. It combines a sequence of first-order approximations into a single practical analysis tool through a telescoping construction. The aim is to make aspects of learning easier to inspect while retaining enough accuracy to provide useful empirical explanations.

Across three case studies, the authors use this model to investigate phenomena including double descent, grokking, linear mode connectivity, and difficulties with tabular data. The construction enables them to extract metrics that help predict and interpret unexpected network performance. These are empirical insights from applying the model, rather than a claim that one formula fully explains every instance of these behaviors.

The model also serves as a teaching and reasoning framework by isolating components of training, including in contemporary complex settings. This makes it useful for considering the effects of architecture and optimization choices. The analysis additionally reveals parallels between neural-network learning and gradient boosting, connecting seemingly different learning procedures through the proposed lens.
neurips-2024-deep-learning-through-a-tel.tldr: A telescoping model built from first-order approximations provides empirical tools for understanding surprising neural-network behavior.

paragraphs: Fluid observations often describe what happens at fixed grid locations, an Eulerian view. Moving fluid structures can be difficult to follow in that representation because their motion is spread across changing locations. DeepLag combines this fixed-grid perspective with a Lagrangian perspective, which follows particles as they move through the fluid.

The model adaptively selects key particles and infers their movement from grid-based observations. It then feeds accumulated information about these particle trajectories back into the evolving global grid features used for prediction. The two views therefore play complementary roles: particle tracking captures motion, while grid features retain the broader description of the fluid.

Tracking selected particles gives an interpretable indication of fluid dynamics and reduces the need to model complex relationships among large numbers of grid cells. The authors report strong performance on three challenging prediction tasks spanning two- and three-dimensional fluids and simulated and real-world data. These findings support combining representations of where fluid is observed and how it moves to improve prediction and efficiency.
neurips-2024-deeplag-discovering-deep-la.tldr: DeepLag improves fluid prediction by combining fixed-grid observations with learned trajectories of selected moving particles.

paragraphs: Traffic-signal controllers often assume continuous access to sensor data from surrounding intersections. Sensor failures and lost data can break that assumption, leaving the controller with incomplete information. DiffLight studies this problem in an offline setting and uses a conditional diffusion model to connect filling in missing traffic data with choosing control actions.

Its Partial Rewards Conditioned Diffusion model combines data imputation and decision-making while preventing missing rewards from interfering with learning. A Spatial-Temporal Transformer captures relationships between intersections and their evolution over time. A separate Diffusion Communication Mechanism supports communication and control when parts of the traffic information are unavailable.

Experiments on five datasets, covering multiple missing-data scenarios, demonstrate that DiffLight can effectively control traffic signals under these conditions. The approach matters because missing observations affect both the description of traffic and the decisions made from it. By treating reconstruction and control as connected tasks, the framework addresses that dependence within a single modeling approach.
neurips-2024-difflight-a-partial-rewards.tldr: DiffLight combines missing-data reconstruction and traffic-signal decisions in a diffusion model conditioned on partially available rewards.

paragraphs: Long-tail recognition involves datasets in which some classes have many examples and others have few. DiffuLT addresses this imbalance by training a diffusion model from scratch on the available dataset and using it to generate a balanced proxy dataset. The generative process uses neither external data nor pretrained model weights.

The authors identify approximately-in-distribution samples as especially useful for improving long-tail classification. These samples differ slightly from the real data distribution and mix information from different classes. DiffuLT uses a feature extractor to encourage their generation during training, then filters out harmful samples during generation. The approach therefore considers which generated examples help recognition, alongside how many examples each class receives.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on CIFAR10-LT, CIFAR100-LT, and ImageNet-LT, with substantial gains over the leading competitors evaluated. Ablation studies examine the pipeline's contributions. Together, the findings support generating useful class-balancing data from the original long-tailed dataset itself, without depending on outside generative knowledge.
neurips-2024-diffult-diffusion-for-long-.tldr: DiffuLT trains a diffusion model solely on long-tailed data to generate useful, balanced training examples for recognition.

paragraphs: Explaining one graph prediction does not necessarily reveal the broader combinations of patterns a graph neural network has learned. GraphTrail targets that broader question with a global, post-hoc explanation method. It takes an already trained black-box model and expresses its predictions through a Boolean formula involving graph or subgraph concepts.

The method first automatically discovers discriminative subgraph concepts using Shapley values. It then applies symbolic regression to construct a human-readable logical formula over those concepts. This connects recognizable graph patterns to combinations of conditions that describe the network's predictions. The pipeline works directly toward a global explanation without relying on individual local explainers.

Experiments across multiple datasets and graph-neural-network architectures report more faithful logical explanations than existing global explainers. Here, fidelity concerns how well the formula matches the model's predictions. The findings suggest that explicit rules can provide a useful account of learned combinatorial behavior, supporting model improvement and potential use in settings where understanding predictions is especially important.
neurips-2024-graphtrail-translating-gnn-.tldr: GraphTrail explains graph neural networks globally by discovering subgraph concepts and fitting logical rules to their predictions.

paragraphs: Constrained nonlinear optimization appears in applications such as power systems, robotics, and wireless networks. Interior point methods are a widely used solution approach, but solving their linear equation systems through matrix factorization is computationally expensive. IPM-LSTM applies learning to this costly internal operation to accelerate the broader optimization process.

The method uses a Long Short-Term Memory neural network to approximate linear-system solutions and inserts that approximation into an interior point method. The resulting approximate solution to the nonlinear program then becomes the starting point for an interior point solver. This creates a two-part workflow: learned approximations generate a useful initial solution, and the solver continues from that warm start.

Experiments include quadratic programs and quadratically constrained quadratic programs. Compared with the default solver, the approach reduced iteration counts by up to 60% and solution time by up to 70%. These are the largest reported reductions, showing that learned intermediate computations can substantially reduce solving effort on the evaluated problems.
neurips-2024-ipm-lstm-a-learning-based-i.tldr: IPM-LSTM learns approximate linear-system solutions to produce warm starts that can substantially accelerate nonlinear optimization.

paragraphs: Planning for long-term returns requires decisions that remain coherent across time. This is challenging when learning from offline trajectories without step-by-step rewards, especially when the model can consider only a limited context. The Latent Plan Transformer addresses this by introducing a latent variable that links a trajectory-generating Transformer with the trajectory's final return.

LPT learns from trajectory-return pairs using maximum likelihood. During training, posterior sampling of the latent variable brings information from sub-trajectories into a consistent abstraction despite the finite context. Before execution, the model infers a latent variable from a desired return. This inferred representation supplies the plan that guides subsequent behavior.

Experiments report competitive results on Gym-Mujoco, Franka Kitchen, Maze2D, and Connect Four, including improved decisions learned from suboptimal trajectories. The model also demonstrates credit assignment, trajectory stitching, and adaptation to environmental contingencies. These findings support latent-variable inference as a strong alternative to prompting with rewards at every step when learning plans from trajectory-level outcomes.
neurips-2024-latent-plan-transformer-for.tldr: LPT learns a latent representation connecting trajectories to final returns and infers that representation to guide planning.

paragraphs: MetaCURL studies reinforcement learning in episodic, loop-free environments whose losses and transition probabilities change over time. Its focus is Concave Utility Reinforcement Learning, which accommodates convex performance criteria over the state-action distributions produced by policies. The resulting nonlinearity prevents direct use of traditional Bellman equations, complicating adaptation to changing environments.

The algorithm runs multiple instances of black-box learning algorithms over different time intervals. It combines their outputs through a sleeping-expert framework, allowing different instances to contribute over their relevant intervals. This arrangement addresses non-stationarity without requiring prior knowledge of when or how the environment changes.

The paper proves optimal dynamic regret under a specific transition-information setting: transition uncertainty and change arise only from external noise independent of the agent's state-action pairs. The method also handles fully adversarial losses, extending beyond stochastic-loss settings. The guarantee shows that interval-based expert aggregation can address changing CURL problems under the stated noise assumption, even with only partial transition information.
neurips-2024-metacurl-non-stationary-con.tldr: MetaCURL combines learners operating over different intervals to obtain optimal dynamic regret for changing CURL environments under specified noise assumptions.

paragraphs: MotionCraft generates video by combining an image diffusion model with motion prescribed by a physics simulation. The motivation is to produce realistic, physically plausible movement without the heavy training associated with video diffusion models. Its zero-shot approach builds on an image generator, such as Stable Diffusion, while using simulation to specify how the scene should move.

The simulation supplies optical flow describing motion. MotionCraft applies this flow to the image model's noise latent space. The authors show that this produces coherent motion while allowing the generator to fill in elements needed as the scene evolves. Applying the flow directly to pixels would instead leave artifacts or missing content in the situations described.

Compared with Text2Video-Zero, the method shows both qualitative and quantitative improvements. These findings support the use of simulated motion within a generative representation to produce finely prescribed, complex dynamics. The approach connects explicit physical motion control with the image model's ability to generate visually consistent scene content.
neurips-2024-motioncraft-physics-based-z.tldr: MotionCraft turns physics-simulation motion into video by warping an image diffusion model's noise latent space.

paragraphs: Multi-object 3D grounding means finding the objects described by a phrase within a point cloud and returning their three-dimensional boxes. The task connects language to spatial scene understanding and is relevant to interaction and robotics. D-LISA addresses it with a two-stage approach that makes both candidate construction and reasoning more adaptable.

Three components define the method. A dynamic vision module learns a variable number of proposed boxes. Dynamic camera positioning extracts features for each proposal. A language-informed spatial attention module then reasons over the proposals to produce the final prediction. Together, these components connect candidate locations, their extracted visual features, and the wording used to identify the desired objects.

Experiments report a 12.8% absolute improvement over state-of-the-art methods on multi-object grounding, while remaining competitive on single-object grounding. The result supports the combined approach for locating multiple language-specified objects. It also indicates that the method's emphasis on multiple candidates can coexist with useful performance when a query concerns only one object.
neurips-2024-multi-object-3d-grounding-w.tldr: D-LISA improves multi-object 3D grounding through adaptive box proposals, dynamic feature extraction, and language-guided spatial reasoning.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object can also require recognizing its state, such as its color or material. The paper argues that incremental learners focus too heavily on object categories and therefore struggle with combinations of states and objects. It introduces Compositional Incremental Learning and reorganizes two existing datasets to support studying this task.

The proposed learner, CompILer, uses several prompt pools and encourages both differences between pools and diversity within each pool. Object prompts guide the selection of state prompts, explicitly connecting the object being considered with its possible state description. The selected prompts are combined through a generalized-mean strategy intended to remove irrelevant learned information.

Experiments on the two adapted datasets report state-of-the-art performance. The contribution includes both a task formulation for learning state-object combinations incrementally and a prompt-based method for handling their ambiguous boundaries. The findings support treating state recognition and object recognition as connected parts of incremental learning, with object information helping determine which state prompts are relevant.
neurips-2024-not-just-object-but-state-c.tldr: CompILer uses object-guided state prompts to learn combinations of objects and their states incrementally.

paragraphs: A model that adapts successfully for a short period may still deteriorate after many updates. This paper investigates that possibility through recurring test-time adaptation, where previously encountered environments return within a long data stream. Repetition makes it possible to examine accumulated errors even when the model revisits familiar testing conditions.

The authors also analyze an epsilon-perturbed Gaussian mixture classifier as a simplified setting for adaptation. This yields theoretical insights into how properties of both the data and the adaptation algorithm contribute to gradual degradation. Building on that investigation, they introduce persistent test-time adaptation, or PeTTA, which detects movement toward model collapse and changes its adaptation strategy.

PeTTA balances continued adjustment with preventing collapse. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate greater stability than the existing methods evaluated in lifelong adaptation scenarios. The findings emphasize that sustained adaptability requires attention to the consequences of repeated updates: responding to the current environment and preserving the model's ability to keep adapting are linked objectives.
neurips-2024-persistent-test-time-adapta.tldr: PeTTA detects signs of model collapse and adjusts test-time adaptation to remain stable as environments recur.

paragraphs: Learning from surgical video and language is difficult because multimodal data is scarce and specialized knowledge is essential. Surgical lecture videos can also lose useful textual information, while procedures unfold across space and time. PeskaVLP addresses these connected problems by enriching language supervision and explicitly learning alignment between language and visual procedures.

A hierarchical knowledge augmentation approach uses large language models to refine and expand surgical concepts. This provides richer supervision and reduces overfitting risk. The pretraining framework combines that language information with visual self-supervision, constructs hard negative samples, and uses a Dynamic Time Warping loss to learn cross-modal alignment across procedural sequences.

Experiments on several public datasets for surgical scene understanding and cross-modal retrieval report significant improvements in zero-shot transfer. The resulting visual representation is intended to serve multiple surgical understanding tasks. These findings support using structured domain knowledge together with temporal alignment when learning from surgical video, where understanding the progression of a procedure matters alongside recognizing visual content.
neurips-2024-procedure-aware-surgical-vi.tldr: PeskaVLP enriches surgical language supervision and learns procedural video-language alignment to improve zero-shot transfer.

paragraphs: Learning problems can change because both data distributions and goals evolve over time. Prospective Learning develops a theoretical framework for this setting, where the best prediction rule may itself change. The paper contrasts this with the largely time-independent treatment in probably approximately correct learning and examines what it means to learn for future data.

The proposed Prospective Empirical Risk Minimization learner returns a sequence of predictors. Roughly, it includes time alongside the usual data inputs, allowing predictions to account for when they will be used. Under specified assumptions on the stochastic process generating the data, the authors prove that its risk converges to Bayes risk.

The paper also shows that standard empirical risk minimization without time can fail to learn under dynamic distributions. Numerical experiments illustrate prospective learning on synthetic problems and visual recognition problems constructed from MNIST and CIFAR-10. The results combine a conditional theoretical guarantee with examples showing why time can be a meaningful part of the prediction problem.
neurips-2024-prospective-learning-learni.tldr: Prospective Learning incorporates time into prediction and proves convergence to Bayes risk under assumptions about the evolving data process.

paragraphs: Some neural-network properties concern relationships between multiple executions. Robustness against a universal adversarial perturbation is one example, because the same perturbation connects the executions being analyzed. RABBit targets these relational properties, where treating executions independently can discard useful constraints and produce imprecise verification results.

The paper identifies two gaps in existing tools. Complete infinity-norm robustness verifiers do not reason about dependencies across executions, while existing relational verifiers use only one bounding step without branching to refine it. RABBit combines branch-and-bound across multiple executions with bound refinement that uses cross-execution relationships. This gives the verifier a way to progressively sharpen its analysis while retaining relational constraints.

Experiments across a broad range of datasets and networks report substantially greater precision than state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution is a scalable relational verification procedure that brings branching and relational reasoning together. The findings show the value of considering dependencies during refinement when the property being checked spans several executions of a network.
neurips-2024-relational-verification-lea.tldr: RABBit improves relational neural-network verification by combining branching across executions with bounds that preserve their dependencies.

paragraphs: Diplomacy requires agents to combine social reasoning, negotiation, and strategy over extended periods. Negotiation greatly expands the space of possible decisions, adding difficulty beyond handling many actions or several game steps. Richelieu explores how language-model agents could integrate the capabilities needed for these complex interactions among multiple parties.

The approach brings together three components. Strategic planning uses memory and reflection to support decisions over time. Goal-oriented negotiation incorporates social reasoning so that interactions remain connected to the agent's objectives. Self-play games expand memory, providing a mechanism for self-evolution without a human participating in that improvement loop.

The significance of this design lies in linking conversation, accumulated experience, and long-term planning within one agent approach. Negotiation is treated as part of pursuing a strategy, while self-play supplies additional experience for memory. The abstract presents this as an exploration of agents capable of comprehensive multi-agent missions; it describes the intended capabilities without reporting a measured performance result.
neurips-2024-richelieu-self-evolving-llm.tldr: Richelieu explores diplomacy agents that combine reflective planning, socially informed negotiation, and memory growth through self-play.

paragraphs: A language model's safety behavior may depend on both the task and the way it is prompted. SG-Bench examines whether safety generalizes across those changes. It addresses two gaps identified in existing benchmarks: separating generative from discriminative evaluation, and relying on standardized inputs that overlook common prompting techniques.

The benchmark combines tasks involving generated responses with tasks involving discrimination or judgment. It also includes data for studying prompt engineering and jailbreak effects, covering influences such as system prompts, few-shot demonstrations, and chain-of-thought prompting. This broader design tests whether safety behavior remains consistent when the interaction format changes.

An evaluation of three proprietary and ten open-source models found that most performed worse on discriminative tasks than on generative tasks and were highly sensitive to prompts. The authors interpret this as poor generalization of safety alignment in the tested models. Their quantitative and qualitative analyses highlight why evaluating one task format or prompt style provides an incomplete picture of safety behavior.
neurips-2024-sg-bench-evaluating-llm-saf.tldr: SG-Bench finds that safety behavior in evaluated language models often fails to generalize across task types and prompting styles.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimal control offers a mathematical account of how perception and action can work together under uncertainty. Realistic sensorimotor modeling includes multiplicative noise in feedback and motor output, together with internal noise in estimation. These noise sources make optimization difficult. The authors identify a problem in a commonly used derivation: its unbiased-estimation property does not hold.

They propose an efficient gradient-descent approach that minimizes future expected cost while imposing only linearity of the control law. The procedure repeatedly propagates sufficient statistics in closed form to calculate expected cost, then optimizes the filter and control gains. This directly connects the treatment of estimation with the choice of actions.

The method achieves significantly lower overall cost than the state-of-the-art solutions evaluated, with especially strong improvements under internal noise and gains in other circumstances as well. The paper also supplies theoretical explanations. Better control solutions matter for inverse control inference, where researchers use observed behavior to infer underlying objectives under assumptions of rational action.
neurips-2024-stochastic-optimal-control-.tldr: The paper corrects an estimation issue and jointly optimizes filtering and linear control to lower costs under sensorimotor noise.

paragraphs: Neuron attribution connects a model's outputs to individual neurons to investigate the semantic information they encode. Although this approach has progressed in text-only language models, its use in multimodal models is less developed. NAM is an attribution method designed specifically to examine how neurons participate in processing and generating content across modalities.

The method reveals modality-specific semantic knowledge and highlights properties described as cross-modal invariance and semantic sensitivity. These properties concern how neuronal behavior relates to meaning across different modalities and how it responds to semantic content. Together, they offer a more detailed view of internal representations than simply observing the model's final output.

The authors support NAM with theoretical analysis and empirical validation. They also use it to introduce a multimodal knowledge-editing paradigm, connecting interpretability with a downstream application. The contribution therefore includes both a way to inspect learned semantic structure and a proposed way to use that understanding when editing knowledge in a multimodal language model.
neurips-2024-towards-neuron-attributions.tldr: NAM attributes multimodal language-model outputs to neurons, revealing semantic properties and supporting a knowledge-editing approach.

paragraphs: Urban knowledge graphs organize information from varied urban data sources, but constructing them requires substantial manual effort. UrbanKGent develops language-model agents for tasks such as extracting relational triplets and completing missing graph knowledge. Its training instructions explicitly account for heterogeneous data and geospatial information relevant to urban settings.

The framework refines action trajectories distilled from GPT-4 through an iterative, tool-augmented module. It then combines these augmented trajectories with instructions to fine-tune models from the Llama 2 and Llama 3 families. The resulting agent family includes versions with 7, 8, and 13 billion parameters.

Evaluation on two real-world datasets uses both human assessment and GPT-4 self-evaluation. The authors report outperforming 31 baselines and exceeding GPT-4 by more than 10% at approximately twenty times lower cost. They also report potential to construct graphs with hundreds of times richer relationships using one-fifth of the existing benchmark's data. These findings support specialized instruction and trajectory training for more efficient urban graph construction.
neurips-2024-urbankgent-a-unified-large-.tldr: UrbanKGent trains specialized language-model agents with urban instructions and refined tool-use trajectories to improve knowledge-graph construction.

paragraphs: Multimodal in-context learning uses examples supplied in a prompt to help a model perform a task without updating its parameters. Its success raises a practical question: which choices about those examples and instructions matter most? This paper studies that question through experiments involving six vision-language models and twenty strategies.

The investigation covers three stages: retrieving demonstrations, ordering their contents and the demonstrations themselves, and constructing the prompt. The findings emphasize the need for multimodal retrieval when choosing demonstrations. They also show that ordering within an individual demonstration matters more than ordering separate demonstrations, and that introductory instructions improve the model's understanding of the task.

These results give concrete guidance for the prompt-design choices examined in the study. Selecting examples, arranging their internal content, and explaining the task all influence how effectively a model uses its context. The work contributes an empirical account of those influences, helping turn multimodal in-context learning from a collection of prompting choices into a more systematically studied procedure.
neurips-2024-what-factors-affect-multi-m.tldr: Experiments identify multimodal retrieval, ordering within demonstrations, and introductory instructions as key factors in multimodal in-context learning.
